lead: V2X means Vehicle-to-Everything: a car exchanges short radio messages with other cars, roadside units, pedestrians' phones, the cloud and the grid. It exists because radar and cameras see only line of sight and cannot know intent; a V2V message can say 'I am braking' before the brake lights are visible. The same electronics unit, the telematics control unit, also feeds navigation, music and over-the-air updates into the cabin. You meet V2X in collision warnings at blind corners and in connected infotainment.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for in-car networks, Chapter 6.3 for Ethernet backbones, and Unit 5 ADAS sensors for radar, camera and LiDAR context.

blocks.text: V2X means Vehicle-to-Everything. It is a set of short radio messages between a vehicle and the world around it. The vehicle carries an on-board unit (OBU), a radio plus a small computer. A fixed roadside unit (RSU) is the infrastructure box at a junction, toll plaza or highway gantry.

The five links are: V2V, vehicle to vehicle; V2I, vehicle to infrastructure; V2P, vehicle to pedestrian, usually a phone app; V2N, vehicle to network, meaning the cellular cloud; and V2G, vehicle to grid, for an electric vehicle that charges or sends power back. V2V and V2I can work without a SIM or tower. Only V2N and cloud services need cellular coverage. Routing among moving vehicles is covered in Chapter 6.7.

A safety message carries position, speed, heading, brake status and a time stamp. From these, the receiving OBU predicts a path. Common warnings are: forward collision warning (the car ahead brakes hard); intersection movement assist (a car is about to cross your path at a blind junction); emergency vehicle warning (an ambulance is approaching); road-hazard alert (a pothole, crash or slippery patch); and green light optimal speed advisory (GLOSA), which tells the driver a speed to reach the next green light. GLOSA advises; it does not control the signal.

blocks.where: d is distance in metres (m); v<sub>rel</sub> is closing speed in metres per second (m/s); t is warning time in seconds (s).

blocks.text: At 40 m/s closing speed and 2.5 s, d = 100 m. Radio latency adds v<sub>rel</sub> × Δt, where Δt is latency in seconds; 100 ms adds 4 m.

sections.h3: Radio choices, TCU and cloud services

blocks.text: Two radio families dominate. IEEE 802.11p is a Wi-Fi-derived link in the 5.9 GHz band. It works ad hoc: an OBU sends a safety packet directly to nearby OBUs without a base station. It has no SIM and no subscription. Its stack is in Chapter 6.8. LTE-V2X is the cellular family. It defines a sidelink, a direct device-to-device radio path, so V2V can run without a tower. When coverage exists, the network can schedule resources. 5G-V2X extends this with lower latency and more capacity, but the safety idea is the same: send small, frequent, authenticated messages. 802.11p is mature and independent of cellular coverage. C-V2X can reuse cellular timing and security, and it can also use the network for V2N.

The telematics control unit (TCU) is the car's cellular gateway. It holds a modem, a GNSS receiver for position and time, and an eSIM. It connects to the in-car network through a gateway. The TCU carries V2N services: live traffic, remote diagnostics, emergency call, stolen-vehicle tracking, tolling and over-the-air (OTA) updates. OTA means the manufacturer sends new software or calibration over the cellular link, so the car need not visit a workshop. A toll plaza may read a tag over DSRC or RFID; the money message goes to the toll backend. The TCU is not the same as the safety OBU, though some cars combine both in one box. A gateway keeps infotainment traffic away from safety-critical CAN or Ethernet domains.

The head unit is the cabin computer behind the dashboard screen. It plays audio and video, runs navigation with live traffic, and projects a phone through Android Auto or Apple CarPlay. Smartphone projection places the phone's apps on the car screen, so the head unit supplies the display, touch and audio while the phone does the computing. Navigation uses GNSS plus map data; the TCU adds traffic and charging-station updates. A head-up display (HUD) may show speed, a turn arrow or a warning on the windscreen. Some syllabi list HUD here; its optics and combiner belong to Unit 2.

The connected cabin widens the attack surface. Attack points include the cellular link, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB ports, the OTA server and the diagnostic connector. A malicious message could fake a brake warning or unlock a door. Message authentication is the main defence for V2X: each safety packet carries a signature and a certificate, so a receiver can check that the sender is a real OBU and that the packet was not altered. Authentication proves origin and integrity; it does not by itself hide the content, and it needs a public-key infrastructure (PKI) to issue and revoke certificates. A gateway, message filtering and separate safety domains add defence in depth.

A connected autonomous vehicle uses V2X as one more input beside radar, camera and LiDAR. Radar measures range and speed; camera reads lanes and signs; LiDAR builds a point cloud. V2X adds information beyond line of sight and, more importantly, intent: 'I am braking' or 'I am turning left'. The fusion unit must weigh a delayed or false V2X message against its own sensors.

examples.question: Two cars close at 40 m/s relative speed. A warning is useful 2.5 s before a possible collision. How far ahead must it arrive, and how much does 100 ms of V2X latency add?
steps: Warning distance without latency: d = v_rel × t = 40 m/s × 2.5 s = 100 m.
Convert latency to seconds: 100 ms = 0.100 s.
Extra distance caused by latency: d_latency = 40 m/s × 0.100 s = 4 m.
Required arrival distance: 100 m + 4 m = 104 m.
examples.answer: The warning must arrive by 104 m; latency adds 4 m to the ideal 100 m.
examples.check:
v = 40.0
t = 2.5
latency_ms = 100.0
d = v * t
extra = v * (latency_ms / 1000.0)
total = d + extra
print(d)
print(extra)
print(total)

traps: V2X is radio communication, not a radar or camera. A car with V2X still needs its own sensors; V2X adds messages beyond line of sight.
V2V and V2I do not need cellular coverage. Only V2N and cloud services stop when the tower is down.
Do not mix 802.11p and LTE-V2X. 802.11p is ad hoc Wi-Fi in 5.9 GHz; LTE-V2X has a direct sidelink plus an optional network mode.
Authentication is not encryption. A signature proves sender and integrity; it may leave the message readable.
Convert 100 ms to 0.1 s before multiplying by m/s. Using 100 gives a 100-times error.

quiz.a: V2I is vehicle-to-infrastructure: an OBU talks to a roadside unit. V2G is vehicle-to-grid: an electric vehicle exchanges power or data with the grid.

quiz.q: Why can V2V work with no cellular coverage?
quiz.a: V2V uses a direct radio link between the two on-board units. It does not need a base station or SIM. Coverage matters only for V2N cloud services.

quiz.q: Car A closes on Car B at 25 m/s. A warning is needed 2.0 s ahead. V2X latency is 80 ms. Find the ideal distance, the extra distance from latency, and the required arrival distance.
quiz.a: Ideal: 25 × 2.0 = 50 m. Latency: 80 ms = 0.08 s, extra = 25 × 0.08 = 2 m. Required arrival: 50 + 2 = 52 m.

quiz.q: Give two reasons V2X needs message authentication and one limit of authentication.
quiz.a: It stops a fake emergency-braking message and a spoofed position that could cause a wrong warning. Limit: a signature proves origin and integrity but does not hide the content, and the system needs a PKI to issue and revoke certificates.

quiz.q: List three safety V2X use cases and say what each warns about.
quiz.a: Forward collision warning warns of a hard-braking car ahead. Intersection movement assist warns of a crossing path at a blind junction. Emergency vehicle warning warns of an approaching ambulance or fire engine.

quiz.q: Compare 802.11p and LTE-V2X on coverage dependency, direct link, and one advantage.
quiz.a: 802.11p is ad hoc and independent of cellular coverage; it gives a direct OBU-to-OBU link. LTE-V2X has a direct sidelink for V2V and can also use network scheduling; its advantage is managed cellular resources and a path to 5G-V2X. 802.11p's advantage is maturity and no subscription.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is moving toward 5G NR V2X, cooperative perception and edge computing at roadside units. Research questions include misbehaviour detection when a real OBU sends false data, and privacy-preserving certificates that still allow revocation. Search for C-V2X sidelink, cooperative awareness message, and V2X public-key infrastructure. The security and latency parts connect to autonomous-vehicle safety cases.
